Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Diana Lopez (Redwood SE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Rachel Kim (Starlake - Head of ML), Jared Owens (Starlake - Platform Eng), Marcus Lee (Starlake - CTO), Priya Nair (Starlake - SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):

Topics:

- Benchmarks and POC plan

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick us off. quick intros?
[00:00:07] Rachel: yeah hi rachel kim here, head of ml at starlake. we run conversational assistants for payments support and fraud triage.
[00:00:14] Marcus: marcus, cto, looking at economics mostly.
[00:00:17] Jared: jared here, platform engineer. we're responsible for infra, networks, and links to our internal k8s clusters.
[00:00:22] Samir: great. diana and ethan from the SE team will run the deep part on batching and the kv cache.
[00:00:28] Diana: hey, quick agenda - we'll show cost model tradeoffs, demo the console Optimize recommendations, and then dig into prefix and kv caching patterns.
[00:00:36] Jared: perfect. our goal is to see if we can cut token costs by >40% without violating our 150ms p95 latency requirement.
[00:00:44] Ethan: ok good, that's clear. quick question - what's your current stack and how are you currently calling the model?
[00:00:51] Rachel: we call gpt-style endpoints through a sidecar service in k8s, most traffic on AWS us-east-1, about 45k req/day, avg prompt length ~200 tokens, 95th output tokens ~120. latency today is typical 250ms p95 and cost is high.
[00:01:08] Diana: thanks. based on that profile, two levers are most important - batching (to increase token throughput per GPU) and caching (prefix cache for static preambles, kv cache for session state).
[00:01:18] [00:01:20] Marcus: can you explain difference between prefix and kv? we heard conflicting terms.
[00:01:24] Diana: sure - prefix caching is storing repeated prefix tokens (like instruction, system messages) so they don't need to be re-encoded on each request. kv cache (sometimes you hear "K V" cache or kv-store) stores the model's key-value attention cache for a session, so subsequent generation doesn't re-compute past context. prefix saves encoder cost, kv saves autoregressive compute.
[00:01:42] Jared: and both affect cost differently?
[00:01:45] Diana: yes. prefix helps when many requests share the same system prompt or few template turns - it's cheap and easy. kv cache is higher memory and can reduce per-token compute a lot if sessions are long and repeated tokens matter. but it requires sticky routing or session affinity and more memory on the serving nodes.
[00:02:05] Samir: quick note, hosts vs dedicated - Hosted we can do prefix caching and some automatic batching, Dedicated gives you more control for larger KV cache sizes and deterministic throughput for heavy session workloads.
[00:02:18] Rachel: our use case is conversational with session context ~800 tokens typical, so kv cache sounds appealing but we're concerned about memory footprint and network.
[00:02:28] Ethan: understood. we ran a similar profile for a payments customer - with 800 token sessions and 50% kv hit-rate we saw 30-45% CPU/GPU token cost reduction depending on batching.
[00:02:40] [00:02:45] Marcus: what's the tradeoff on latency for batching windows? we can't add too much latency.
[00:02:50] Diana: right - batching has a tradeoff: larger batching windows increase throughput (better GPU utilization) but add queueing latency. Redwood Optimize suggests dynamic batching with max queue window, e.g., 5-15ms default for low-latency apps; if you need sub-100ms p95 we keep windows small and rely more on KV to reduce per-token compute.
[00:03:12] Jared: sounds like we need to know exact numbers. do you have a cost model?
[00:03:16] Diana: yes, we prepared a spreadsheet - i'll walk through high-level here. assumptions: model open-llm-3-small (example), average input tokens 200, output tokens 120, throughput target 80 req/s during peak. We evaluate baseline (no cache, conservative batching), prefix-only, kv-only (50% hit), both combined.
[00:03:40] Diana: baseline per-token GPU cost is X (in spreadsheet it's translated to $0.0021 per 1k tokens for that model on our hosted). prefix-only reduces encoding work ~20-30% depending on prefix length, kv-only reduces autoregressive compute proportional to hit-rate and cached history length. combined can achieve >40% cost reduction in many configs.
[00:03:59] Rachel: those numbers are helpful - can you share the spreadsheet after?
[00:04:02] Samir: absolutely, i'll send it. link is in the notes, and diana will share a cleaned copy with your specific inputs.
[00:04:08] [00:04:12] Marcus: how stable are hit-rate estimates? our sessions vary a lot.
[00:04:16] Diana: hit rates depend on user behavior. for payments assistants where users follow guided flows, you often see high prefix reuse and decent local cache hits. we recommend instrumenting a short sampling run for 7 days to measure real reuse and feed those values into the cost model.
[00:04:32] Jared: question about deployment: we have strict network rules - we need VPC and SAML SSO and audit logs; would Dedicated or Private be preferable?
[00:04:40] Samir: short answer - Private (VPC) gives you the most control - full customer-managed networking and optional on-prem. Dedicated can be placed in partner regions with VPC peering and still meet many security needs, and Hosted also supports encrypted transit and SOC2 controls but if you require full VPC egress controls, Private is the way.
[00:05:00] Rachel: ok. what about data retention for cache - do you keep KV on disk?
[00:05:04] Diana: KV cache is in-memory for performance on the serving nodes; for longer lived sessions you can snapshot state to a KV store (customer-managed or ours) but for PII concerns we recommend keeping cache ephemeral and controlling retention via config. Redwood supports KMS integration and audit logs for any snapshotting.
[00:05:21] [00:05:25] Marcus: any constraints on model choice or quantization? we plan to use an LLM with 8-bit quant and client-side sharding.
[00:05:31] Ethan: Redwood runtime supports quantized kernels and has quantization profiles. with 8-bit you'll get lower memory per KV entry but watch impact on latency. our Optimize suggestions will include quantization tradeoffs in the spreadsheet.
[00:05:46] Jared: what about session affinity - we can't always route to same GPU for sticky sessions.
[00:05:50] Diana: you can do a hybrid approach - keep short sticky windows at the region level and use a shared remote KV store for cold sessions. For high hit-rate cases, Dedicated pools with session pinning deliver best hit-rates and lower cross-node traffic. We also support fallback to stateless mode if session is not found, with instrumentation for miss rates.
[00:06:12] Samir: i'll add that we have routing policies - can prefer low-latency nodes, and automatically fallback to smaller models if capacity constrained.
[00:06:20] Rachel: good - we might also want an A/B test to measure quality regressions with quantization.
[00:06:24] Diana: absolutely - Optimize ties quality monitoring to prompt sets so you can detect regressions post-quantization or model swap.
[00:06:31] [00:06:34] Ethan: i'll show a quick screenshot of the Optimize cost model in the console - bear with me. (screen share noise)
[00:06:40] Ethan: you can see baseline cost per 1k tokens, different rows for prefix/hit-rate, and a simulated weekly spend. there's a column for latency impact for each config.
[00:06:50] Marcus: can you export inputs? we want to plug in our own traffic pattern.
[00:06:54] Diana: yes the spreadsheet is parameterized - you paste your RPS, token distribution, expected kv hit-rate, and it outputs expected monthly cost and cost delta. diana: we'll send a version prefilled with your numbers.
[00:07:06] Rachel: great. a technical nit - how is the KV cached key computed? we want deterministic keys to avoid collisions.
[00:07:13] Diana: keys are a hash of session_id + conversation_turn_id + optionally a short canonicalization of the prompt. collisions are extremely unlikely; for extra safety you can namespace keys per-customer.
[00:07:25] Jared: about memory sizing - what's the rough per-session overhead?
[00:07:28] Ethan: rough rule: KV entry size roughly proportional to sequence length * hidden_dim * bytes-per-float. with quantization you reduce bytes-per-float. in spreadsheet we show examples: 800 token session at fp16 ~ ~120MB of KV, with 8-bit quant it's closer to 30-40MB. this is approximate and model-dependent.
[00:07:50] [00:07:55] Marcus: that's significant. we likely need Dedicated with larger memory or a hybrid approach.
[00:07:58] Samir: yep that's common for fintech customers - dedicated pools or on-prem nodes sized for KV-heavy workflows.
[00:08:05] Rachel: what about fallback behavior if KV node evicts entries?
[00:08:08] Diana: Redwood supports TTLs and eviction policies; when an entry is missing, the system falls back to re-sending the full context (stateless) or using a prefix-only path. We recommend monitoring miss rates and tuning cache sizes.
[00:08:20] Jared: could you run a small benchmark for us - say a 2 hour run with our sample prompts?
[00:08:25] Samir: yes, that's part of the POC. we'll need your prompt sample and a traffic emulator. we'll run hosted and dedicated sims to compare costs and latency.
[00:08:34] Rachel: perfect. next, about security - SAML/SSO + audit logs + SOC2. do you have SOC2 cert?
[00:08:40] Samir: yes we are SOC2 compliant, and we have SOC2 report redacted for security review. also support SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integration for key management. i'll share our security whitepaper.
[00:08:52] [00:08:56] Marcus: any gotchas for peering with our VPC? we have strict egress rules and a private subnet.
[00:09:00] Ethan: we'll coordinate with your network team; Dedicated and Private have options for VPC peering and private links. sometimes customers need to open a small set of outbound ports for health checks; we'll document them.
[00:09:11] Jared: ping - we also do strict PCI scoping in our infra, so any data that touches Redwood must be scoped.
[00:09:16] Samir: understood - for PCI-sensitive workloads we recommend Private on-prem or air-gapped packages; we'll flag that in the follow-up.
[00:09:25] [00:09:30] Diana: ok back to cost model - i want to highlight two realistic configs: low-latency mode (queue window 5ms, small batch sizes, kv hit-rate 40%), and cost-optimized mode (queue window 25ms, bigger batches, kv hit-rate 60%). low-latency gave ~20-25% cost reduction, cost-optimized gave ~45-55% in our tests.
[00:09:52] Rachel: how do you measure kv hit-rate in prod? instrumentation?
[00:09:56] Diana: yes - Redwood emits cache hit/miss metrics at token and session granularity, with traces to link misses to user flows. we can surface that in the Console and export into your telemetry.
[00:10:07] Marcus: think about monitoring - we need tracing down to token-level, especially for false negatives.
[00:10:12] Ethan: Console supports trace hooks and integrates with OTLP/Jaeger.
[00:10:17] Jared: any limits on concurrent KV sessions per node? we have bursts of many users.
[00:10:21] Diana: cluster sizing depends on memory per session; the Optimize sheet has a node sizing tab - you input expected concurrency and it suggests node counts and memory.
[00:10:31] [00:10:35] Rachel: ok good - can you share an example of a customer that did this?
[00:10:39] Diana: yes, we ran mariner-payments last year - they reduced monthly spend by ~48% after a 2-week POC by combining prefix caching and 8-bit kv with dedicated pools. i'll link the case study.
[00:10:50] Samir: quick handoff to next steps - we'll send spreadsheet, security docs, pricing, and propose a POC kickoff once you provide sample prompts and traffic.
[00:10:58] Marcus: timeline preference - we want to align with Q2 budget review. ideally pilot starts before end of March.
[00:11:04] Samir: doable, we'll aim for that.
[00:11:07] Jared: one final - do you support function/tool calling and structured outputs with caching?
[00:11:12] Diana: yes - you can cache prefixes even with structured tool calls, though tool outputs may need custom canonicalization. kv still helps for conversation state between tool calls.
[00:11:23] [00:11:25] Rachel: thanks. wrap up?
[00:11:27] Samir: recap - Samir send pricing & SOC docs, Diana send cost-model spreadsheet and example node sizing, Starlake provide 7-day traffic sample and 3 canonical prompts, schedule POC kickoff.
[00:11:41] Marcus: sounds good.
[00:11:43] Jared: i'll loop in our security folks after you send the docs.
[00:11:47] Samir: perfect - any other questions?
[00:11:49] Rachel: none from me. thanks all.
[00:11:52] Samir: thanks everyone.
